I always pick my software based on the communities behind them, and you should to. Whatever you use, that is what you are supporting, you are casting your vote. Nobody wants to work on something if the work will go unnoticed. Every download hit a distribution gets, every install is a win for the developers. For the open source community, it's not about the amount of money that can be made, it's about the amount of people that will make use of.

I used Suse as my primary OS up until the Novell purchase, and ditched it completely after the Attachmate group purchased Novell. I toyed with RedHat, but the 2000-2005 era when Fedora was born was sort of a migration period for large entities(this was also when openSuse was born). This was really when the separation of supported software and community software evolved into it's current state. This is around the time Ubuntu was born. Mark Shuttleworth, an entreprenuer that had done some development for Debian decided to launch his own distribution. He initially dumped 10 million into his project. I latched on, loved it. But with the birth of Unity, so died my love for Ubuntu.

I now use Linux Mint, it is what Linux was always meant to be. What us open source nerds always wished and hoped it could be back in the 90s. Plug n' Play, a full operating system out of the box, but still with options to go full on nerd if you feel like dicking around in the terminal.

It actually brings me a great deal of sadness, the whole systemd debacle. Those new to Linux might not truly understand, but Debian has always been kind of a beacon for everything Open Source values. I mean shit, they wouldn't even include Firefox without modifying it because of trademarked Mozilla artwork.

Now if you are new to open source, you're probably also wondering why people keep shouting Slackware. Slackware is the oldest linux distro currently in development (being actively maintained). The same developer runs it, Patrick Volkerding, and he is to distribution-level as Linus Torvaldes is to kernel-level. He has not deviated his distro for anyone, he is not a sell out, he most likely will never sell out, and his distro is rock solid. Installing Slackware is like hitting the rewind button on Linux and going back to the 90s, it is definitely not Plug N' Play. However, if you are wanting to support a distribution that you can be 100% sure deserves your support, Slackware is definitely at the top of the list. No matter what anyone says.
